column2: they turn back without reaching him; yet he is denoted by the one syllable. From the one syllable called a, the self called Brahma is named;
from the one syllable called u, Vidya, Vishnu, is proclaimed; from the one syllable called m, Shiva is declared as Rudra.
From Mahesha's right side was born Brahma, called the self; from his left side arose Vishnu, therefore called Vidya;
from the heart of Shiva arose Nilarudra, called Shiva. Brahma sets creation in motion, Vishnu preservation, the deluder,
and Rudra likewise dissolution; he is always the controller of those two.
The nada, of the nature of the half measure, is heard at the head of the linga; though that supreme syllable, the pranava, was then divided,
Therefore those three are called the causes of the world, and Shiva, cause of the three causes, is the supreme cause.
Since you two, bound in enmity by rajas, did not understand this meaning, the linga appeared between you to awaken you.
Thus they call me "Om," as the Atharva has said here; the Riks, Yajuses and Samans and other branches by the thousands —
even though the Vedas themselves declared it clearly thus with their own mouths, it was not grasped by the two, like something experienced in a dream.
To awaken them there and to remove their darkness, all was imprinted on the linga too, just as the Vedas declared it.
Seeing that imprinted on the linga, by the grace of the bearer of the linga, the two gods then became calm in mind and awakened.
The origin, dissolution and true nature of the six paths; the abode higher than that, and the Person who possesses that abode,
the Brahman beyond the highest, Shiva the Lord without parts, ever the master of this manifold world made of the bound and the noose,
free of fear from any quarter, utterly without growth or decay, imperishable, pervading outside and inside, yet beyond outside and inside,
beyond excess, eternal, distinct from all the worlds, without marks, indescribable, beyond the range of speech and mind,
for discernment the two gods understood nothing. Then the unmanifest pranava was transformed into the form of the Vedas.
of the single essence of light, peaceful, gracious, ever risen, abode of all welfare, joined with a Shakti of like kind —
knowing the god Virupaksha, Brahma and Narayana then, placing their folded hands on their heads, spoke in fear.
Brahma said: "Ignorant or knowing, I was made by you in the beginning, O God; if I have fallen into such delusion, who is at fault here?
Leave aside this ignorance of mine; when you are present, lord, who could speak without fear of his own task or another's?
Even our dispute, O god of gods, was fortunate, since it gave the fruit of bowing at the feet of you, our lord."
Vishnu said: "O God, no speech is equal to praising your greatness; yet before the lord, silence on the part of his servants would be a transgression.
What is fitting to do here — only that suits the occasion. Not knowing, I have babbled something and bow to you.
The causal role you gave me I forgot through your maya; deluded and full of ego, I have now been corrected again.
What need of many words? I am greatly afraid, O Lord, since I set out to measure you, the immeasurable.
They call you Mahadeva, destroyer of the distress of the fearful; therefore, Shankara, please forgive my transgression today."
There the a became the Rik, the u the imperishable Yajus, the m became the Saman, and the nada the Atharvan Shruti.
Addressed thus by those two lords, Maheshvara, pleased, favoured the two gods and spoke with a smile.
The Lord said: "Child, child, Brahma, Vishnu, deluded by my maya, proud in your lordship and bound in enmity to each other,
you quarrelled even to the point of battle and did not stop; thereby the creation of creatures was broken off, you who are the causes of the world,
through the discord arising from your ignorance and pride. To stop that, your pride and delusion were checked by me myself
today, by the play of the linga's appearance. Therefore, giving up dispute and shame entirely,
perform your own tasks, free of envy. Long ago, by my command, together with all the collections of knowledge,
I gave you, for the establishment of your causal role, the supreme jewel of mantras called the sutra, made of five syllables.
All that I taught you, you have forgotten today; I give it all again as before, by my command,
since without it you two are unable to create and protect." Having said this, Mahadeva gave Narayana and the Grandsire
the king of mantras together with the collection of knowledge. Having received the great, divine and supreme command of Maheshvara,
This Rik established in brief its own meaning: Brahma among the rajasic qualities, the first among the forms and among the acts,
the jewel of mantras of great meaning and likewise all the kalas, they prostrated like staffs at the feet of the god of gods,
and stood then, free of fear, motionless with bliss. Meanwhile, wondrously, like a magic show, the Lord's
linga vanished somewhere and could no longer be perceived by them. Then, lamenting "Alas!" at the sudden breaking of their love,
and saying to each other, "What wondrous thing has happened?", reflecting on the inconceivable glory of Shambhu, they were freed from distress.
Entering into supreme friendship and embracing each other, the two chief gods departed, intent on the work of the world.
From then on all gods and asuras headed by Shakra, the sages, men, nagas and women too, install lingas according to rule and worship him in the linga.
creation among the worlds, the earth among the principles, the imperishable self, Nivritti on the path of kalas, and Sadya among the five Brahmans;
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 36: the description of the rite of installation. Shri Krishna said: Lord, I wish to hear the excellent rite of installation of the linga and of the image as ordained by Shiva.
Having made one of metal or wood, marked with a lotus seat, he should place in the middle a large pedestal-shrine.
Worshipping the four doorkeepers beginning with Bhadra in order — Subhadra, Vibhadra, Sunanda and Vinandaka —
having bathed and worshipped the linga together with its pedestal, and wrapped it all around with two cloths with kusha tufts,
he should gently bring it to water and lay it on the pedestal, with its head to the east, its thread below, and its base to the west.
He should keep the linga there overnight with every auspicious thing, for five nights, three nights, or one night.
Having taken out what was worshipped there and purified it as before, and worshipped it in festival fashion, he should bring it to the sleeping-house.
There too he should make a sleeping place in the middle of a mandala; bathing the linga with pure water, he should worship it in order.
Drawing a lotus in the north-east on a purely plastered ground, and purifying a Shiva pot, he should invoke Shiva there and worship.
Having arranged a white lotus in the middle of the altar according to rule, he should also draw a lotus of Chandika to its west.
Making a bed on it with new cloths of linen and the like, or flowers or darbha, he should place a golden flower there.
Upamanyu said: On a day not unfavourable to oneself, in the bright fortnight, one should make a linga of proper measure by the path described in the Shiva shastra.
Bringing the linga there with all auspicious sounds, wrapping it all around with a pair of red cloths with a kusha tuft,
together with its base, he should lay it down as before. Drawing a lotus in front, on its petals in order
he should place the Vidyesha pots, and the Shaiva vardhani in the middle. Excellent brahmins should make offerings around the three lotuses.
They should be arranged as the eight forms, stationed around from the east; or four in the directions, reciters with Vedic learning.
They should make offerings, and are remembered as the four forms beginning with Viranchi. The teacher, first of them, in the north-east or the west,
should perform the principal offering with the seven substances in order; other brahmins should offer a quarter or half of the teacher's.
Or the guru alone may perform the principal offering here. First, having offered the full oblation, and a hundred and eight oblations with ghee,
he should place Shiva's hand on the head of the linga with the root mantra. Having offered fifty or twenty-five with the seven substances in order,
after each offering he should touch the linga and the pedestal again and again; then, offering the full oblation, he should give fees in order:
to the officiants a quarter or half of the teacher's, and to the architect too; half of that should be given to others and to the members of the assembly according to his means.
Then, having chosen an auspicious site and examined the ground, he should perform the ten services, preceded by the drawing of the marks.
Then, placing a golden bull or a kusha tuft in the pit, he should lay the Brahma stone in the pit, purified with clay-water, the five cow products and again with pure water,
and anointed with sandal. Then, performing the placing on the hands with the nine names of the Shaktis,
he should put orpiment and other minerals, with seeds, perfumes and herbs, on the Brahma stone according to the rule described in the Shiva shastra.
Having set up a proxy linga made of a milky tree and knowing it to be stable, he should remove it and set the linga on the Brahma stone,
inclining slightly to the north-east, with the root knowledge; then joining the pedestal, remembering the Shakti root mantra,
making it fast with binding substances and purifying the spot, giving arghya and flowers, they should again draw the curtain.
Then, before the linga, the sprinkling and the rest as is fitting; bringing the pots from the sleeping place, he should place them in order.
Beginning the great worship and worshipping the ten pots, remembering Shiva's mantra, into the water of the Shiva pot
with thumb and ring finger joined taking it, he should utter it; the mantra-knower should place it in the middle of the Ishana part of the linga.
Likewise he should place Shakti, Vidya and the Vidyeshas in order at the root of the linga, and then sprinkle the linga with the Shiva water,
For those ten services, having first worshipped Vinayaka and purified the site and the rest, he should take the linga to the bathing-house.
the pedestal with the vardhani, and the linga again with the Vidyesha pots; having sprinkled, he should then arrange the seat beginning with the support.
Having performed the placing of the five kalas, he should remember the linga as blazing, and with folded hands, facing north-east, invoke Shiva and his consort in person:
remembering the god coming with the Goddess from the sky, mounted on the king of bulls or a celestial chariot, adorned, rich with the splendour of every ornament, with all auspicious sounds,
surrounded on all sides by gods and danavas headed by Brahma, Vishnu, Mahesha, the Sun and Shakra, all their limbs moist with bliss, their folded hands on their heads,
praising, dancing and bowing. Then, having worshipped with the five services, he should conclude.
There is no rite higher than this with the five services. He should perform installation in images too everywhere as for the linga.
At the time of drawing the marks, the opening of the eyes should be done; in the water-dwelling and in the bed he should lay the images face down,
and with mantras he should join to its heart the image laid in the pot-water. They call installation when the temple has been built the higher, rather than before it is built.
One who is able should perform the installation rite after the temple is built; if unable, having installed the linga or image,
he should afterwards build a Shiva temple according to his ability. And I shall tell the excellent rite of installation for household worship.
With a golden stick dipped in saffron and other juices he should then draw the prescribed marks according to the shastra of craftsmen.
Having made a smaller image, or a linga with the proper marks, when the northern course has come, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day,
making an altar in an auspicious place, he should draw a lotus there as before; scattering leaves, flowers and the like, and placing a pot in the middle,
he should place four pots around it in the directions; placing the five Brahmans with their seeds in those five, with the five,
worshipping them, showing the gestures and the rest and protecting them, purifying the linga or image with clay-water and the like as before,
he should place it, covered with flowers, on an excellent seat to the north. Placing a flower on its head, he should sprinkle it with the sprinkling water;
worshipping it again with flowers, preceded by cries of victory and the like, he should bathe it with the pots from Ishana to Vidya, with the root knowledge.
Then, having performed the placing of the five kalas and the worship as before, he should daily worship there the three-eyed god with the Goddess.
Or, placing a single pot with the mantra of the form within the lotus, he should do all the rest as before.
A linga badly defiled should be purified and installed again; a defiled one should be sprinkled; a slightly defiled one should be worshipped.
The lingas called bana may or may not be installed, since they have already been consecrated by Shiva himself.
With the waters of the eight clays, or likewise with the waters of five clays, he should purify the linga together with its pedestal and with the five cow products.
The rest that are seen like bana lingas are to be installed. For a self-manifested linga, and likewise for a divine one or one established by sages,
if it has no pedestal, placing a pedestal and performing the rite of sprinkling, one should worship Shiva there; installation is not prescribed for them.
A burnt, loose or damaged linga should be cast into a body of water; one fit to be repaired should be repaired and the rite of installation performed.
From a damaged image or linga, preceded by worship of the god, he should dismiss the god into his heart and perform the rejoining or the abandonment as fitting.
If the worship is interrupted for one day he should perform double worship; for two nights, a great worship and then sprinkling.
If worship is interrupted for many days beyond a month, some prescribe installation, others the course of sprinkling.
In the sprinkling of a linga and the like, dismissing the god as before, bathing it with clay-water in the order of eight and five,
bathing it with the cow products and purifying it with darbha water, he should sprinkle it with the sprinkling water a hundred and eight times with the root mantra.
Placing his hand with flowers and kusha on the head of the linga, he should recite the root mantra five times, a hundred and eight and more.
Then with the root mantra he should touch it from the head down to the pedestal, and perform a great worship, invoking the god as before.
Having worshipped it with its pedestal, taking it to a divine or other body of water, he should keep the linga with its pedestal there overnight,
If no installed linga is available, he should worship the blessed Shiva at a place of Shiva, in water, in the fire, in the sun or in the sky.
in a pure dwelling for the overnight rite, with every adornment, with arches and enclosures, surrounded by garlands of darbha,
furnished with the eight elephants of the quarters and the eight pots of the guardians of the directions, with the eight auspicious objects, and with the guardians of the directions worshipped.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 37: the description of the course of yoga. Shri Krishna said: Extracting the essence of knowledge, ritual and conduct in summary, you, lord, have told everything, and I have heard it, equal to the Shruti.
since the universe is contemplated as a form whose parts have dissolved; the yoga of non-being is declared, from the non-appearance of a real thing.
The nature of Shiva alone, without adjuncts, is contemplated; such a Shaiva state of mind is here called the great yoga.
He whose mind is dispassionate toward objects seen and heard of has eligibility for yoga, and no one else.
From seeing the faults of both kinds of objects and the qualities of the Lord, the mind always becomes dispassionate.
All yoga in brief is eightfold or sixfold: restraint, observance, postures such as the svastika,
breath-control, withdrawal, concentration, meditation and samadhi — these eight limbs of yoga are told by the wise.
Posture, restraint of breath, withdrawal, concentration, meditation and samadhi are in brief the six limbs of yoga.
Their separate characteristics are described in the Shiva shastra, and in other Shiva Agamas, especially the Kamika and the rest,
and likewise in the yoga shastras and in some Puranas. Non-violence, truth, not stealing, celibacy and non-possession are called restraint by the good, as five members.
Purity, contentment, austerity, japa and devotion — observance has these five kinds by its own divisions.
Now I wish to hear of yoga, most hard to attain, with its eligibility, limbs, rules and purpose,
Svastika, padma, ardhendu, vira, yoga, prasadhita, paryanka and yatheshta — posture is declared eightfold.
Prana is the air born in one's own body; its ayama is restraint. It is said to be threefold: rechaka, puraka and kumbhaka.
Pressing one nostril with a finger, one should expel the air of the belly through the other; this is remembered as rechaka.
One should fill the body with outer air like a bellows through the other nostril; from filling it is held to be puraka.
He neither releases nor takes in the air inside or outside, but stays full like a pot, unmoving; that is kumbhaka.
These three beginning with rechaka, neither fast nor slow, the practitioner of yoga should practise with effort in due order.
The practice of rechaka and the rest, preceded by the purification of the channels, up to voluntary departure from the body, is declared in the teaching of yoga.
The restraint of breath-control, in the order beginning with the lowest, is taught as fourfold by the division of measures and qualities.
The lowest is of four kinds, of twelve measures; the middle, of two ascents, is of twenty-four measures;
the highest, of three ascents, is of thirty-six measures; beyond that is the breath-control that produces sweat, trembling and the like.
If there is death before, without the disruption of yoga and the rest, how can it be accomplished at once so that the man is not a self-slayer?
The arising of bliss, horripilation, shedding of tears from the eyes, babbling, whirling, fainting and the like arise in the yogi at the highest.
Circling the knee, neither fast nor slow, one should snap the fingers; that is declared a measure.
Measures are to be known in order by the order of ascents; one should practise breath-control preceded by the purification of the channels.
Breath-control is remembered as twofold, agarbha and sagarbha: without japa and meditation it is agarbha, and with them sagarbha.
Breath-control with them is more than a hundred times greater than without; therefore yogis practise sagarbha breath-control.
By the conquest of prana alone the airs of the body are conquered: prana, apana, samana, udana and vyana,
naga, kurma, krikala, devadatta and dhananjaya. Since it causes movement, it is called prana;
the one called apana leads downward the food and the like that is eaten; vyana pervades and nourishes all the limbs;
the air that agitates the vital points is called udana; since it brings all the limbs to evenness, it is sung as samana.
Naga is said to be in belching, kurma in the opening of the eyes, krikala is to be known in sneezing, devadatta in yawning;
and that, and its cause, and its time and means, and the gradations of its kinds — please tell me truly.
and all-pervading dhananjaya does not leave even the dead body. This breath-control, practised in order and in due measure,
burns up every fault and protects the practitioner's body. When prana has been properly conquered, one should observe its signs:
then there is a lessening of faeces, urine and phlegm, the capacity to eat much, and breathing after long intervals,
lightness, swiftness, enthusiasm, a fine voice, the destruction of all diseases, strength, radiance and good looks,
steadiness, intelligence, youthfulness, firmness and serenity. Austerities, the destruction of sin, sacrifices, giving, vows and the like
do not equal a sixteenth part of that breath-control. The senses attached here each to their own objects —
drawing them back and restraining them is called withdrawal. The senses headed by the mind, and heaven and hell —
restrained or let loose, they lead to heaven or to hell. Therefore the wise man seeking happiness, resting in knowledge and dispassion,
should quickly restrain the horses of the senses and lift up the self by the self. Concentration, in brief, is binding the mind to a place;
and the place is Shiva alone, nothing else, since the rest has the three faults. The mind set in a place for a certain time,
Upamanyu said: You have asked fittingly, Krishna, knowing the meaning of all questions; therefore I shall tell it all in order — listen attentively.
not straying from its target — that is concentration, and nothing else. The first steadiness of the mind arises from concentration;
therefore one should make the mind steady by practising concentration. The root dhyai is remembered in the sense of thinking; thinking of Shiva again and again
with an undistracted mind — that is called meditation. The like succession of thought of a mind established on the object of meditation,
free of other thoughts, is called meditation. Giving up everything else, Shiva alone, the bringer of good,
the supreme lord of gods, is to be meditated upon — so ends the Atharvan Shruti. So too Shiva's consort, supreme, is to be meditated upon; the two, Shiva and his consort, are in all beings.
They are heard in the Shrutis and smriti shastras as all-pervading, ever risen, all-knowing, always to be meditated upon in their various distinct forms.
Liberation is the first thought and the powers beginning with anima the other; thus the purpose of this meditation is to be known as twofold.
The meditator, meditation, the object of meditation and the purpose of meditation — knowing these four, the knower of yoga should practise yoga.
Endowed with knowledge and dispassion, full of faith, forbearing, without sense of "mine" and ever energetic — such a man is remembered as a meditator.
Tired of japa, he should meditate again; tired of meditation, he should do japa again; for one engaged in japa and meditation, yoga is quickly accomplished.
The steady state of the mind fixed on Shiva, when its other modifications are restrained, is in brief yoga, and it is fivefold:
Concentration is twelve breath-lengths; meditation twelve concentrations; up to twelve meditations is called samadhi.
Samadhi is declared the last limb of yoga; through samadhi the light of wisdom shines everywhere.
That in which only the object shines forth, which stands like a still ocean, a shining as if empty of its own form — is called samadhi.
Setting the mind on the object of meditation, he should see it very steadily; the yogi like an extinguished fire is said to be in samadhi.
He does not hear, smell, speak or see, does not feel touch, and his mind does not form intentions;
he identifies with nothing and is not bound, like a log; one thus merged in Shiva is here said to be in samadhi.
As a lamp in a windless place never flickers, so the wise one established in samadhi should not waver from it.
For the yogi who thus practises the excellent yoga for long, the obstacles to it, the wise say, gradually all perish.
the yoga of mantra, the yoga of touch, the yoga of feeling, and the yoga of non-being; above them all the great yoga is held to be supreme.
The undistracted state of mind whose object is the meaning denoted by the mantra, through the power of mantra practice, is declared the yoga of mantra.
That same, headed by breath-control, is called the yoga of touch; freed from mantra and touch, it is declared the yoga of feeling;
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 38: the description of the arising of obstacles on the course of yoga. Upamanyu said: Sloth, severe diseases, negligence, doubt about the place, instability of mind, lack of faith, erroneous vision,
Intuition, hearing, tidings, sight, taste and sensation — these six are the disturbances, the powers of yoga in its expenditure.
The true shining forth of an object that is subtle, hidden, past, remote or future is called intuition.
Hearing is the hearing of all sounds without effort; tidings is the understanding of the talk of all embodied beings.
Sight is the seeing of divine things without effort; likewise taste is said to be the tasting of divine flavours.
Likewise the perception of touch is renowned as sensation, and of divine smells and the like. The lords of the worlds up to Brahma
stand by and give many jewels; free, sweet and varied speech flows forth;
all elixirs and divine herbs become available; divine women bow to him and offer themselves.
When even a part of the power of yoga is seen, the mind turns to liberation: "As I have seen this, so will liberation be."
Thinness, stoutness, childhood, old age and youth, the forms of various species, the bearing of the bodies of four,
and constant holding of fragrant scent without the earthy portion — thus they speak of the eightfold earthy state of the pishachas.
sorrows, dejection and fickleness toward objects — these ten are declared the obstacles of men practising yoga.
Dwelling in water and likewise emerging from the earth; being able, if he wishes, to drink up even the ocean himself without harm,
seeing water wherever he wishes in this world, holding a mass of water in the hand without a pot or the like,
whatever tasteless thing he wishes to eat becomes at once flavoured and so on, bearing the bodies of three,
and the body free of wounds, together with the earthy powers — this sixteenfold watery lordship is wonderful.
Producing fire from the body, freedom from fear of its heat, the power to burn this world without effort if he wishes,
placing fire in water, holding fire in the hand, cooking food in the mouth as before when creation is burned, the creation of bodies of two, with the watery powers —
this they declare the twenty-fourfold fiery lordship. Swiftness of mind, entering within beings in an instant,
bearing great weights such as mountains without effort, heaviness and lightness, holding the wind in the hand,
making even the earth tremble with the touch of a fingertip and the like, producing a body of one, with the fiery enjoyments —
the poets know this as the thirty-twofold lordship of the wind. Producing one without a shadow, the invisibility of the senses,
Sloth is the heaviness of body and mind of yogis; diseases are faults arising from imbalance of the humours and from the faults of karma.
moving through the sky at will, union with the objects of the senses, crossing space, and placing it within one's own body,
making space into a ball, bodilessness, together with the lordship of wind — this great fortyfold one
is called the lordship of Indra, and they declare it of space. Obtaining whatever one wishes, going out wherever one wishes,
overpowering all, seeing all secret things, creation according to karma, control, a pleasing appearance,
and seeing worldly existence, with Indra's enjoyments — this lunar lordship is mental and greater in qualities.
Cutting, striking, binding and releasing, seizing all beings under the sway of worldly existence,
favour to all, and victory over death and time — this lordship of self-identification they call that of Prajapati;
with the lunar enjoyments this great one is fifty-sixfold. Creation by mere will, protection and destruction,
authority over all, setting in motion the minds of beings, the unlikeness of all, creating a world apart,
making good and evil, joined with the powers of Prajapati — they call this the sixty-fourfold lordship of Brahma.
Negligence is failing to cultivate the means of yoga; doubt about the place is knowledge beset by "Is it this or that?"
Beyond this lordship of intellect, they know the secondary lordship of nature; it is called Vaishnava, and the maintenance of the worlds is his; that whole state cannot be told by Brahma or others.
That of Purusha, the secondary, the state of the lord of the ganas, the Lord's — something of that state cannot be known even by Vishnu or others.
The powers of knowledge are all disturbances; they are to be restrained with effort through supreme dispassion.
For one whose mind is attached to impure appearances and qualities, the supreme lordship, fearless and fulfilling all desires, is not accomplished.
Therefore whoever abandons like straw the qualities and enjoyments of gods, asuras and kings attains the supreme perfection of yoga.
Or the sage, wishing to show grace to the world, may wander about; having enjoyed qualities and enjoyments at will, he will go to liberation.
Now I shall tell the practice of yoga; listen attentively. At an auspicious time, in an auspicious place, such as a holy field of Shiva, secluded, free of creatures, silent and free of disturbance,
on well-plastered ground, pleasant, scented with fragrance, incense and the like, strewn with loose flowers, adorned with canopies and the like,
furnished with kusha, flowers, fuel-sticks, water, fruits and roots; not near fire or water, nor on a heap of dry leaves,
not where there are gnats and mosquitoes, snakes and beasts of prey, not full of wild animals, not in fear, not surrounded by the wicked,
Lack of footing of the mind is called instability; lack of faith is an attitude devoid of feeling on the path of yoga;
not in a cremation ground, at a shrine or anthill, in a ruined house, at a crossroads, on the bank of a river, stream or ocean, or in a street,
not in a ruined garden, a cowpen or the like, not in an unpleasant or reviled place, not with indigestion or sour belching, nor defiled by faeces and urine,
not with vomiting or diarrhoea, not after overeating or when tired, not very troubled with worry, nor very hungry or thirsty,
nor engaged in duties to one's guru and the like, should one practise yoga. Moderate in food and recreation, moderate in effort in one's tasks,
moderate in sleep and waking, free of all strain, on a seat that is soft, lovely, ample, level and clean,
he should practise among the postures such as padma and svastika. Having saluted in order those to be saluted, ending with his own guru,
with neck, head and chest erect, he should not sit with eyes tightly shut; with head slightly raised, he should not let his teeth touch;
placing the tongue motionless behind the tips of the teeth, protecting the testicles and the organ with the heels,
placing the arms crosswise on the thighs without strain, placing the back of the right hand on the palm of the left,
raising the back gently and holding the chest forward, gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking about in the directions,
the mind that is perverted is called error. They know sorrow born of ignorance as the mental affliction of men, relating to the self;
the movement of his breath gathered, motionless like a stone, contemplating within the shrine of his own body Shiva with Amba,
he should worship with the sacrifice of meditation in the middle of the pedestal of the heart-lotus. At the root, the tip of the nose, the navel, the throat, the palate or the openings,
between the brows, at the door, on the forehead or the head, he should remember them, having duly arranged the supreme seat of Shiva and his consort,
with enclosures or without; in a two-petalled, sixteen-petalled or twelve-petalled lotus according to rule,
or in a ten-petalled, six-petalled or four-petalled one he should remember Shiva. Between the brows is a two-petalled lotus, blazing like lightning;
of the lotus between the brows, in order, on the right and left petals, of lightning colour, are the last letters;
the petals of the sixteen-petalled one are the sixteen vowels, from the east in order; this lotus is at the root of the bulb.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 39: the description of Shaiva yoga. Upamanyu said: Thinking that for those who remember lord Shrikantha the accomplishment of every aim comes at once, some yogis meditate on him.
At the end one should make it objectless and seedless, for every accomplishment. Through breath-control the Goddess's powers beginning with Shanti are accomplished in order:
Shanti, Prashanti, Dipti, and then Prasada. The calming of all calamities is called Shanti;
the destruction of darkness within and without is sung as Prashanti; the light within and without is called Dipti;
the soundness of the intellect is declared Prasada. And all the instruments, outer and inner,

quickly become serene through the serenity of the intellect. The meditator, meditation, the object of meditation and the purpose of meditation — knowing these four, the meditator should practise meditation.
One endowed with knowledge and dispassion, ever undistracted in mind, full of faith and serene of self, is declared by the good to be a meditator.
The root dhyai is remembered in the sense of thinking; thinking of Shiva again and again
Even a little practice of yoga destroys sin, as does meditating even for a moment with faith on the supreme Lord.
with an undistracted mind is called meditation.
The support of this meditation, which is a stream of the intellect, is called by the good the object of meditation, and that is Shiva himself with Amba.
Some practise gross meditation for the steadiness of the mind; in the gross the mind becomes still, and in the subtle it becomes firm.
The thought of liberation and full lordship such as anima are directly declared to be the purpose of complete meditation on Shiva.
Since from meditation one obtains both happiness and liberation, therefore, giving up everything, a man should be devoted to meditation.
There is no knowledge without meditation, and no meditation for one without yoga; he who has meditation and knowledge has crossed the ocean of existence.
Knowledge, serene, one-pointed, free of all limiting adjuncts, is accomplished only for the yogi engaged in the practice of yoga.
The mind turns to knowledge and meditation in those whose sins are entirely destroyed; for those whose understanding is struck by sin, even talk of it is very rare.
As a greatly blazing fire burns dry and wet, so the fire of meditation burns good and evil karma in an instant.
As even a very small lamp destroys great darkness, so even a little practice of yoga destroys great sin.
The very great good that comes to one who meditates on the supreme Lord with faith even for a moment has no end.
There is no holy place equal to meditation, no austerity equal to meditation, no sacrifice equal to meditation; therefore one should practise meditation.
Yogis do not resort to holy places full of water or to gods of stone and clay, because of their conviction in their own self.
When Shiva is contemplated directly, all powers are accomplished; when other forms are meditated upon, one should contemplate Shiva's form.
For yogis the subtle body of the Lord becomes directly visible, as for those not joined in yoga the gross one fashioned of clay, wood and the like.
As here the king's inner attendants are dear to him and not the outer ones, so those devoted to inner meditation are dear to Shambhu, not those devoted to rites.
As outer labourers in the world do not greatly share in the fruit, seen in a king's palace, so here too are those devoted to rites.
If one who has set out for the yoga of knowledge perishes midway, by the mere effort toward yoga he will go to the world of Rudra.
Having experienced happiness there, he is born in a family of yogis; regaining the yoga of knowledge, he passes beyond worldly existence.
The goal that a man attains even by desiring to know yoga, he does not attain by all the great sacrifices.
The fruit gained by worshipping ten million brahmins learned in the Veda is gained by giving merely alms to a Shiva-yogi.
Whatever fruit there is in sacrifices, the agnihotra, gifts, holy places and fire offerings, one obtains all that fruit by giving food to yogis.
